doc.title: Shelly Berg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Clients who can't describe music: Debussy and the turtle
summary: Stories of directors and producers misdescribing what they want, including the Debussy-versus-Mozart story and an aquatic turtle cue, plus commercial trends.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Sometimes. You can think you’re right on the wavelength and you’re totally wrong. It’s gotten to where sometimes I’ll just say can you give me an example of something that’s what you mean. Because they can say something and the words that they are using evoke a certain thing but it’s really the opposite of what they want. There’s a famous film scoring story of a well known composer, who the director said for this one cue, give me Debussy, I want Debussy.

It’s a true story. He gets on the scoring stage and he’s got LaMer nailed. And it’s gorgeous and the textures, and the cellos with five different parts. And he finishes and the orchestra is all tapping their bows, and the director walks up to him and says, “You know, I hate it. I just hate it.” So at that point the director said, “I want my mother” I think that’s the quote, that’s what he said, I want my mom. But he got with the director and what the composer found out was that the director really wanted Mozart. He just threw out the first classical name he could think of, which was Debussy. But the sound he had in mind was Mozart.
It’s all the same thing, isn’t it?

Yeah. So the second T.V. series that I wrote for I did a children’s series for two years on ABC. And the very first episode there was a turtle in the episode. The kid in the episode had a pet and I wrote this little piece of music. And the producer comes in and I thought she was joking, she said, “You know that music’s not quite working, you’ve written land

turtle music and that’s really an aquatic turtle.” I thought she was joking. I said, “Well you had it in an terrarium, you faked me out here, I thought it was a land turtle. She was serious. I had to change the music and somehow figure out what she meant by water turtle music.

It’s really fascinating to watch the trends that commercials seem to jump on. Like I’ve been noticing lately a lot of commercials that have a female vocalist imitating Sheryl Crow. And this seems to be the hot thing. And I wonder how long that will last, until something else comes along.

Well it’s because one of them worked. And that’s the big thing in the media these days. Anything that works, let’s just do that because it’s already proved itself. And it can be frustrating when you’re composing because it puts you in a very narrow box. But it’s a gig.
